value.overview: The Great Shearwater is a large oceanic seabird of the petrel family. It breeds on a few remote islands in the South Atlantic and spends much of the nonbreeding season over the North Atlantic, traveling thousands of kilometers between hemispheres. It is powerful in flight, using long glides and wind-assisted arcs above waves. Although it is included on Costa Rica’s bird list, it is an accidental and exceptionally rare visitor rather than a regular coastal species.
value.classification: The Great Shearwater belongs to the order Procellariiformes and family Procellariidae. Its scientific name is Ardenna gravis; older literature often used Puffinus gravis or the common name Greater Shearwater.
value.identification: This is a large shearwater with long, narrow wings, a heavy dark bill, and a broad, blunt-looking tail. Adults have a dark gray-brown cap and upperparts, a contrasting white collar and face, and white underparts marked by brownish smudging on the belly and underwings. The flight is strong and purposeful, with long glides on stiff wings close to the sea. Its size, dark cap, white collar, and belly smudges help separate it from similar shearwaters.
value.rangeHabitat: Great Shearwaters breed on Gough Island, islands in the Tristan da Cunha group, and Kidney Island in the Falkland Islands. Outside the breeding season they range widely across the Atlantic, from southern waters north toward the Arctic. They use open ocean, continental-shelf waters, fronts, and areas where prey concentrates. In Costa Rica, the species is recorded only as an accidental or extremely rare visitor, most plausibly in offshore Caribbean waters; it is not a regular bird of either Costa Rican coast.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance trans-equatorial migrant. It breeds in the South Atlantic, then moves north into the North Atlantic during the boreal summer before returning south. Costa Rica lies outside its normal migration corridor, so occurrences there are accidental and very uncommon, with no established seasonal passage pattern.
value.breeding: Great Shearwaters breed colonially on remote, predator-free or predator-limited South Atlantic islands. They nest in burrows or sheltered cavities among grass and other island vegetation. Adults return to colonies, court, and mate before females lay a single egg. Both parents share incubation and chick-rearing duties. The chick remains at the nest while the adults forage at sea, and breeding colonies are visited only during the species’ South Atlantic breeding season.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small fish and squid, along with crustaceans and other marine prey. Great Shearwaters often forage where prey is concentrated near the surface, including productive ocean fronts and shelf waters. They may feed in groups, follow marine predators, seize prey while sitting on the water, and take discarded fish or offal around fishing vessels. Their hooked bill and strong swimming ability help them handle slippery prey.
value.behavior: Great Shearwaters are highly pelagic and spend most of their lives at sea. They are usually seen singly or in loose flocks, sometimes gathering around feeding activity created by fish schools, cetaceans, or fishing boats. In flight they alternate strong wingbeats with long glides and can soar and wheel in strong winds. They rest on the water between feeding bouts and come ashore mainly to breed.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable, although monitoring is limited and population estimates are not equally strong across all breeding colonies.
